summary.text: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's velocity or shape, or resist other forces.
Force has both a size and a direction, and it is measured in newtons.
Early thinkers believed force is needed to keep things moving; Galileo and Newton showed it is needed to change motion.

facts.label: Kind of quantity
facts.value: A vector: size and direction both matter

facts.label: Equilibrium
facts.value: Net force on a body is zero

items.prompt: Centuries ago, a thinker watched a cart stop soon after the ox quit pulling. What wrong conclusion did this lead people toward?

options.label: That a force is needed just to keep something moving
That a cart only stops when it reaches its natural speed
That friction is what makes carts start moving
That heavy loads need no force to be moved at all

items.explain: Aristotle's view held that continued force keeps motion going, partly because friction is easy to overlook.

items.prompt: Two people push the same crate with equal strength from opposite sides. Why does it stay put?

options.label: Equal pushes combine into one much stronger push
Forces have direction, so the opposing pushes cancel out
The crate's weight blocks either push from working
A push only counts when one side is stronger

items.explain: Force is a vector, so opposing forces can add to zero net force, which means equilibrium.

items.prompt: Galileo rolled stones and cannonballs down a slope. What did their motion show about gravity?

options.label: It sped the heavier ones up much more than the light ones
It sped up only the ones that were rolling the fastest
It sped them up by the same amount, whatever their mass
It sped them up only until they reached a set speed

items.explain: The bodies accelerated independently of their mass, which disproved the Aristotelian theory of motion.

items.prompt: Which of the four known basic interactions is the weakest?

options.label: The weak interaction
Electromagnetism
The strong interaction
Gravity

items.explain: The four interactions are listed in order of decreasing strength, ending with gravitational.

items.prompt: A worker slides a heavy box up a long ramp instead of lifting it straight up. What does the ramp trade away?

options.label: It uses less work, because the box never really rises
It uses less force, but the force acts over a longer distance
It uses more force, but the force acts over less distance
It uses the same force, but over a much shorter path

items.explain: A simple machine gives a mechanical advantage: less force in exchange for acting over greater distance, for the same amount of work.

items.prompt: A mechanic wants to change how fast a wheel spins. Which version of force does that job?

options.label: Stress
Equilibrium
Torque
Momentum

items.explain: Torque is the rotational version of force and changes an object's rotational speed.

beats.title: Why Things Keep Moving
beats.hook: For about two thousand years, smart people believed something about motion that every cart and ice rink seems to confirm, and it was wrong.

beats.prompt: A puck glides across very smooth ice and nobody touches it. What happens to its velocity?
beats.explain: Galileo argued that objects retain their velocity unless a force, such as friction, acts on them.

choices.label: It speeds up because nothing is holding it back
choices.feedback: With no force acting, nothing changes its velocity, up or down.

choices.label: It slows right away because motion needs a continued push
choices.feedback: This is the old view: everyday carts stop, but friction is the hidden force doing it.

choices.label: It holds the same velocity until a force such as friction acts on it

beats.prompt: Put these contributors to the idea of force in order of when they worked.

items.label: Aristotle explains motion with natural places
Galileo rolls stones down an incline
Einstein extends force to near light speed

beats.explain: Galileo corrected Aristotle in the 17th century, Newton's laws came in 1687, and relativity arrived in the early 20th century.

beats.prompt: Match each term to what it describes.
beats.explain: Each is part of how classical mechanics measures and describes force.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: A cart soon halts once the horse stops pulling.
The rough road is applying friction against the cart.
So the halt proves that motion itself needs a continuing push.
On very smooth ground, the same cart would coast much farther.

beats.explain: Friction is a force that changes the cart's motion, so the stop does not show that steady motion needs a push.

beats.idea: A force changes an object's motion; it is not needed to keep steady motion going.

paragraphs.heading: What a force is
paragraphs.text: In physics, a force is an action that can change how fast or in what direction an object moves, or change its shape. A force can also resist other forces, or alter the pressure in a fluid. It turns everyday ideas of pushing and pulling into exact mathematics. Both its size and its direction matter, so force is a vector quantity. It is measured in newtons (N) and often written with the letter F.

paragraphs.heading: Forces at work in mechanics
paragraphs.text: Force sits at the heart of all three of Newton's laws of motion. Common kinds include elastic forces, friction, contact or normal forces, and gravity. Torque is the turning version of force, and it changes how fast something spins. Inside a solid body, each part pushes and pulls on its neighbours, and the spread of those forces is called internal stress. When the forces on a body add up to zero, the body is in equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: An old mistake
paragraphs.text: Ancient thinkers such as Aristotle and Archimedes studied forces, but kept some basic errors. A central one was the belief that motion needs a force to keep going, even at a steady speed. Part of the reason was a poor grasp of friction, a force that is not always easy to notice. Aristotle split motion into natural motion, such as heavy things falling, and forced motion, which needed a force applied all the time. That matched everyday experience, like the steady push needed to keep a cart rolling, but not an arrow, which keeps flying after the archer lets go. Aristotle suggested the air moved aside by the arrow carried it along.

paragraphs.heading: Galileo turns it around
paragraphs.text: Galileo rolled stones and cannonballs down a slope to disprove Aristotle's theory of motion. He showed that gravity sped them up by the same amount whatever their mass. He also argued that objects keep their velocity unless a force such as friction acts on them. This idea, that force changes motion rather than keeps it going, was refined by Isaac Beeckman, René Descartes and Pierre Gassendi, and became a key principle of Newton's physics.

paragraphs.heading: Newton's laws
paragraphs.text: In 1687 Isaac Newton published his great book, the Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica. In it he set out three laws of motion that still shape how physics describes forces today. Nobody improved on them for more than two hundred years. The first law says that a body at rest tends to stay at rest, and a body moving at a steady speed in a straight line tends to keep doing so.

paragraphs.heading: The modern picture
paragraphs.text: Relativity and quantum mechanics revise the laws of motion so that force comes, in the end, from fundamental interactions. Only four main ones are known: from strongest to weakest, the strong, electromagnetic, weak and gravitational interactions. In the Standard Model of particle physics, forces are carried by exchanged particles called gauge bosons. Observations in the 1970s and 1980s showed the weak force and the electromagnetic force to be two faces of one deeper electroweak interaction. Even so, the classical idea of force stays useful for practical work.
